summary: Defines a framework and information model for a Common Log Format for SIP servers, similar to the logs produced by web servers like Apache and proxies like Squid. Common logs help administrators troubleshoot and let tool writers analyze traffic.

eli5.summary: Every shop writes receipts differently. This says that phone-call servers should write their notes in one shared style, so helpers can read them easily.

questions: what is sip common log format
how should sip servers log events
what fields are in a sip clf record
why not use syslog for sip logs
subtitle: A framework and information model for logging SIP traffic in one shared format, like the web's Common Log Format.

tldr.problem: Every SIP product writes logs in its own proprietary format, so support staff cannot easily trace a call across vendors or build common analysis tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC argues for a SIP Common Log Format and defines an information model: the minimum set of fields every log record MUST contain. It leaves the actual record syntax to other documents.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6873 is named as one example of a representation format that follows this model. The log is for troubleshooting and analysis, not billing, QoS measurement or lawful intercept.

facts.label: Timestamp
facts.value: Seconds and milliseconds since the Unix epoch

facts.label: Provisional response delay
facts.value: 1xx if final response delayed more than 200 ms

today: RFC 6872 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines only the information model; the RFC names RFC 6873 as an example of a representation format.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Servers write log records as part of normal work. Web servers such as Apache and proxies such as Squid use a Common Log Format (CLF), and the RFC credits a good part of Apache's success to the fact that third parties could write tools around it. The Apache example it shows has fields for remote host, date, request line, status and bytes.

The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) has no common log format. A typical enterprise deployment mixes SIP entities from several vendors, each logging in a proprietary format, so staff cannot easily trace a call from one entity to another. The RFC also asks that the log be easy to search with command-line text tools, quick to scan, and not require extra libraries on every platform.

The SIP CLF is inspired by the Apache one, but SIP transactions are much more involved than HTTP ones. This document supplies the problem statement and an information model of the minimum headers and fields to log. It does not prescribe a representation format; RFC 6873 is given as an example of one, based on UTF-8.
sections.eli5: If every toy store wrote its receipts in a different way, nobody could build a tool to read them all. This RFC asks phone-call software to agree on one receipt style.

sections.title: What SIP CLF Is and Is Not
sections.content:
The SIP CLF is a standardized way to produce a log file that SIP clients, servers, proxies and back-to-back user agents (B2BUAs) can all use. It holds enough information for people and programs to relate separate transactions and to search for a dialog or a related set of transactions. Its delimited fields make it quick to parse, and it is platform and operating system neutral.

The RFC is explicit about what it is not. It is not a billing tool, because it records events at the signaling layer only and does not check them against the media layer. It is not a quality of service measurement tool, since it does not summarize media events. And it is not a tool for supporting lawful intercept.
sections.eli5: The log is a diary of who called whom and what was said at the doorbell. It does not tell you how good the conversation sounded or how much to charge for it.

sections.title: Why Not Use Something Else
sections.content:
The sipclf working group looked at four alternatives and concluded that each has drawbacks that rule it out as a SIP CLF.

  • Call Detail Records (CDRs): built mostly for charging, so they record things like public user identities that may not match the From and To headers, and their sequence numbers may not match CSeq. That makes it hard to rebuild a dialog. CDRs are also typically made by proxy-like or B2BUA entities, whereas SIP CLF is light enough for a plain user agent, including phones.
  • Packet capture tools such as Wireshark and tcpdump: they do not remove the need for agreed fields, are not easily searched with text tools, need capture libraries on every platform, and cannot decrypt TLS traffic.
  • Syslog (RFC 5424): it defines a packet format and transport but no storage format. The collector's file mixes messages from many originators, a mobile phone may find no collector, and sending every SIP log message is undesirable.
  • IPFIX: it aggregates packets into flows, but it is not a logging format and produces no file for ad hoc text processing.
sections.eli5: The authors checked other ways to keep records, like photographing every letter or mailing notes to a central office. Each had a problem, so they asked for a dedicated log instead.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC lists reasons a common format helps: a common reference for interpreting events from multiple vendors, common tools for trend analysis and traffic reports, and session correlation across the servers a request passes through. It also names message correlation across transactions (for example, all messages for a server transaction, including forked branches) and across dialogs (for example, by Call-ID, From tag and To tag).

Other uses are trend analysis, training anomaly detection systems on log data rather than raw packets, testing SIP equipment by parsing its logs, cursory troubleshooting (for example, how long a final response to an INVITE took), offline analysis, and real-time monitoring. The RFC notes that tracing a request is considerably easier when all servers are in one administrative domain.
sections.eli5: With one shared style, a repair person can follow a phone call from the first house to the last, and a computer can learn what normal looks like and notice when something is odd.

sections.title: Why SIP Is Harder to Log Than HTTP
sections.content:
A SIP entity behaves in a more complex way than an HTTP one. Parallel or serial forking can produce several final responses, and delays between a request and its final response complicate what to log. SIP also groups transactions into a dialog, and they can arrive far apart: a BYE usually arrives long after the matching INVITE was handled and removed from the transaction list, yet the log should still relate them.

ACK needs care. It is tied to INVITE only and gets no response. If it acknowledges a non-2xx response it is part of the original INVITE transaction; if it acknowledges a 2xx response it is a separate transaction of a request only. CANCEL is also tied to an INVITE, but it does get a final response.

RFC 3261 tells a server transaction to send a 1xx provisional response if the final response is delayed for more than 200 ms. The log needs to include those, because they help anomaly detection systems and human observers. The format should also cover B2BUA behavior, which varies with the kind of B2BUA.
sections.eli5: A web request is like asking one question and getting one answer. A phone call is a long conversation with ringing, answering, maybe several phones ringing at once, and a goodbye much later. Logging all that takes more care.

sections.title: The Information Model
sections.content:
This is the core of the RFC. It defines the mandatory fields that MUST occur in every SIP CLF record. Each field, including meta-fields like Timestamp and Directionality, has a maximum size of 4096 bytes, and a logged message body MUST fit that limit too. How bodies are logged is left to the representation format, since bodies may not be valid UTF-8. Optional fields, such as the Reason-Phrase or vendor-specific data, are also left to the representation format.

The mandatory fields are Timestamp (seconds and milliseconds since the Unix epoch), Message type (R for request, r for response), Directionality (s sent, r received), Transport, source and destination address and port, From and From tag, To and To tag, Callid, CSeq-Method, CSeq-Number, R-URI, Status, Server-Txn and Client-Txn. URI parameters should not be logged for From and To, but the R-URI keeps them.

The last two fields, Server-Txn and Client-Txn, tie together the transactions of forking proxies and B2BUAs. An implementation can reuse the topmost branch-id of the incoming request as the server transaction identifier, or generate a locally unique string. Client-Txn can reuse the value placed in the topmost Via branch parameter on forking, or a generated one.

The model applies to all SIP entities. The fields for a proxy apply equally to a B2BUA, and those for a UAS apply to registrars and redirect servers. Every field must appear in every record, so the representation document MUST define how to mark a field as not applicable (for example, R-URI in a response) and how to mark one that could not be parsed. A proxy forwarding a request fills both Client-Txn and Server-Txn, whereas it fills only Client-Txn when creating a record for a request it originates.
sections.eli5: Every note in the diary must answer the same list of questions: when, who sent it, who got it, what kind of message, and which conversation it belongs to. If a question does not apply, you put a dash.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows records using only the mandatory fields, with a dash for fields that do not apply. The cast is Alice and her user agent, proxy P1 (also Alice's registrar), proxy P2 for Bob's domain, and two instances of Bob's user agent, one on IPv4 and one on IPv6, all on port 5060.

Four scenarios follow: a UAC registration (Alice's REGISTER sent, then a response logged), a direct call from Alice to Bob (INVITE, 180 Ringing, 200 OK, then ACK), a call through P1 as seen from the proxy's log, and a forked call where P2 sends the INVITE to two endpoints, one accepts, and P2 sends a CANCEL to the other.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows what the diary pages would look like for a simple sign-in, a direct call, a call passed along by a helper, and a call that rings two phones at once.

sections.title: Security and Privacy of Log Files
sections.content:
A log reveals the state of the entity that wrote it and the nature of what it logged. Log files SHOULD be protected with restrictive file and directory permissions, and operators SHOULD consider measures like disk encryption and restricted physical access. Threats while stored include an attacker viewing or copying the file, and deleting parts of it. An attacker who can read the file but cannot eavesdrop on the network can mount replay or other attacks. Encrypting the SIP traffic does not help, because the entity decrypted the messages before logging them.

Moving logs across the network has its own threats: viewing, modifying or inserting records, removing records, or a man-in-the-middle delivering a falsified file. Operators SHOULD require mutual authentication, channel confidentiality and channel integrity, which SSH or TLS provide. Fields such as IP addresses and URIs can still leak sensitive information, so before logs cross domains operators SHOULD anonymize or obfuscate them. A specification for doing that interoperably is left for further study.

The RFC also warns that logging more fields costs time, disk space and more potentially sensitive data, and that entries can be unbounded in length, so implementers must take care with buffers. Operators should plan for file rollover and periodic retrieval of logs; operational guidance itself is out of scope.
sections.eli5: A diary of everyone's calls is private. Keep it in a locked drawer, and if you send it to someone, use a locked box and cross out names first.

items.label: When
items.desc: Seconds and milliseconds since the Unix epoch.

items.label: R or r
items.desc: R for a request, r for a response.

items.label: s or r
items.desc: s for sent, r for received by the SIP entity.

items.label: Transport
items.desc: Transport used, per the transport rule in RFC 3261.

items.label: Sender
items.desc: IPv4 or IPv6 address and port of the sender.

items.label: Recipient
items.desc: Address and port of the recipient.

items.label: Caller
items.desc: From URI without URI parameters, and its tag.

items.label: Callee
items.desc: To URI without URI parameters, and its tag (absent in the initial request).

items.label: CSeq
items.desc: Method and number from the CSeq header.

items.label: Client transaction
items.desc: Ties client transactions to a server transaction when forking.

Not easily text-searched, needs libraries, cannot read TLS

Aggregates flows, not a text log
Defines the common fields; format is left to other documents
